::: {.objectives}
**Goals.** Prepare a track for `moveHMM`; fit a 2-state model; read its
output properly; decode and map the states; compare 2 and 3 states; check
pseudo-residuals; and segment Leo's migration a different way.

**Time:** ~55 minutes. **Packages:** `moveHMM`, `amt`, `dplyr`, `tidyr`,
`lubridate`.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(moveHMM)
library(amt)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(lubridate)
```
:::


## Task 1 — Prepare the data

An HMM needs **regular** sampling and **contiguous** sequences. That is exactly
what the bursts from Class 3 give us.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
clean <- read.csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(id = individual.local.identifier,
            t  = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
            x  = location.long, y = location.lat) |>
  filter(!is.na(x), !is.na(y)) |>
  distinct(id, t, .keep_all = TRUE)

trk_hr <- make_track(clean, x, y, t, id = id, crs = 4326) |>
  transform_coords(crs_to = 32736) |>
  nest(data = -id) |>
  mutate(data = lapply(data, \(d) {
    d |> track_resample(rate = hours(1), tolerance = minutes(10)) |>
      filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3)
  })) |>
  unnest(cols = data)

# Each burst is an independent sequence: that is what moveHMM calls an "ID"
hmm_in <- trk_hr |>
  filter(id %in% c("Cilla", "Toni")) |>
  transmute(ID = paste(id, burst_, sep = "_"), x = x_, y = y_)

pd <- prepData(as.data.frame(hmm_in), type = "UTM", coordNames = c("x", "y"))

summary(pd$step)
#>     Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max.      NAs 
#>     0.00    39.25   163.72   290.19   381.02 63102.52       28
sum(pd$step == 0, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 9
```
:::


::: {.callout-important}
## Two things to notice before fitting

**Zero step lengths.** A gamma distribution has zero density at zero, so any
exact zero makes the likelihood infinite. `moveHMM` handles this with a
**zero-mass** parameter per state — but only if you supply initial values for
it, otherwise you get
`Wrong number of initial parameters -- there should be 6`.

**A 63 km step.** That is the spatial outlier we found in Class 3. An HMM will
happily invent a "teleporting" state to accommodate two bad fixes. Remove them.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
max(pd$step, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 63102.52
sum(pd$step > 5000, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 2

bad_ids <- unique(pd$ID[which(pd$step > 5000)])
pd <- pd[!(pd$ID %in% bad_ids), ]

nrow(pd)
#> [1] 9264
round(max(pd$step, na.rm = TRUE))
#> [1] 4166
```
:::


## Task 2 — Fit a 2-state model


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(42)

m2 <- fitHMM(
  pd, nbStates = 2,
  # mu1, mu2, sd1, sd2, zeromass1, zeromass2
  stepPar0  = c(50, 500, 50, 500, 0.01, 0.001),
  # angle mean1, mean2, concentration1, concentration2
  anglePar0 = c(0, 0, 1, 3)
)

m2$mle$stepPar
#>                state 1      state 2
#> mean      15.329068722 3.442721e+02
#> sd        12.809771062 3.277368e+02
#> zero-mass  0.004750669 6.629104e-09
m2$mle$anglePar
#>                 state 1     state 2
#> mean          3.0776184 -0.01864526
#> concentration 0.3153941  0.76486144
m2$mle$gamma
#>           [,1]      [,2]
#> [1,] 0.5390064 0.4609936
#> [2,] 0.1190586 0.8809414
```
:::


### Your turn

**2a.** Describe the two states in words.
**2b.** What is the expected dwell time in each?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
round(m2$mle$stepPar, 3)
#>           state 1 state 2
#> mean       15.329 344.272
#> sd         12.810 327.737
#> zero-mass   0.005   0.000
round(m2$mle$anglePar, 3)
#>               state 1 state 2
#> mean            3.078  -0.019
#> concentration   0.315   0.765

gam <- m2$mle$gamma
dwell <- 1 / (1 - diag(gam))
round(dwell, 2)
#> [1] 2.17 8.40
```
:::


**State 1** — mean step of about 15 m with very low angular concentration and
a mean turning angle near π: the animal barely moves and reverses direction
constantly. This is an *encamped* state: resting, ruminating, or grazing
within a very small patch.

**State 2** — mean step of a few hundred metres, mean turning angle near 0 and
higher concentration: **directed movement**.

Dwell times: roughly 2 hours in the encamped state and about 8 hours in the
moving state. Note that these are in **hours** only because the data are
hourly — the units of a dwell time are always "number of sampling intervals".


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
states <- viterbi(m2)
round(table(states) / length(states), 3)
#> states
#>     1     2 
#> 0.215 0.785
```
:::


::: {.callout-warning}
The model has given you *state 1* and *state 2*. Calling them "resting" and
"travelling" is an **interpretation**, and everything above is consistent with
several other stories. To make the labels a measurement rather than a guess
you would need external evidence: accelerometer data, direct observation, or
known activity patterns.
:::
:::

## Task 3 — Decode and map


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
pd$state <- factor(viterbi(m2))

one <- pd[pd$ID == names(sort(table(pd$ID), decreasing = TRUE))[1], ]

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(one$x, one$y, type = "l", col = "grey70", asp = 1,
     xlab = "Easting (m)", ylab = "Northing (m)", main = "Track coloured by state")
points(one$x, one$y, col = c("#1f6f78", "#c1440e")[one$state], pch = 16, cex = 0.5)
legend("topleft", c("state 1 (encamped)", "state 2 (moving)"),
       col = c("#1f6f78", "#c1440e"), pch = 16, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)

plot(one$step, type = "h", col = c("#1f6f78", "#c1440e")[one$state],
     xlab = "Step index", ylab = "Step length (m)", main = "Step length by state")
```

:::

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(m2, ask = FALSE, plotCI = FALSE, plotTracks = FALSE)
#> Decoding states sequence... DONE
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768}
:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-2.png){fig-align='center' width=768}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip}
The second plot is the one to inspect most carefully: it overlays the
**state-dependent densities** on the histogram of your data. If the coloured
curves do not add up to the shape of the histogram, the model has not
described your data and nothing downstream is trustworthy.
:::

## Task 4 — How many states?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m3 <- fitHMM(
  pd, nbStates = 3,
  stepPar0  = c(30, 200, 800, 30, 200, 800, 0.01, 0.001, 0.001),
  anglePar0 = c(0, 0, 0, 0.5, 1, 3)
)

data.frame(states = c(2, 3), AIC = c(AIC(m2), AIC(m3)))
#>   states      AIC
#> 1      2 151969.4
#> 2      3 150777.9
round(m3$mle$stepPar, 1)
#>           state 1 state 2 state 3
#> mean         17.1   187.3   569.1
#> sd           14.9   138.5   398.7
#> zero-mass     0.0     0.0     0.0
```
:::


### Your turn

**4a.** AIC prefers 3 states. Should you report 3 states?
**4b.** What would make you confident that a third state is real?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
round(m3$mle$anglePar, 2)
#>               state 1 state 2 state 3
#> mean             3.06     0.0   -0.05
#> concentration    0.20     0.9    0.66
round(1 / (1 - diag(m3$mle$gamma)), 2)
#> [1] 2.12 3.02 3.40
round(table(viterbi(m3)) / nrow(pd), 3)
#> 
#>     1     2     3 
#> 0.253 0.415 0.332
```
:::


AIC is **lower** for 3 states, and it would very likely keep falling for 4 and
5. That is what mixture models do: extra components always improve the fit to
the shape of the data, whether or not they correspond to behaviours.

Ask instead:

1. **Are the states distinct?** If two states have overlapping step-length
   distributions and similar turning angles, the model has split one behaviour
   in two.
2. **Are the dwell times plausible?** A state occupied for a single step at a
   time is a statistical artefact, not a behaviour.
3. **Is any state rare?** A state holding 2% of steps is usually absorbing
   outliers.
4. **Does it survive?** Refit on a different individual, or a different
   season. A real behaviour recurs; an artefact does not.

Here the third state sits between the other two, which is biologically
reasonable for a large grazer (rest / graze / travel) — but you should say
that you chose 3 for *that* reason, not because AIC said so.

**Report the simplest model that answers your question and passes its
checks**, and state your criterion in the methods.
:::

## Task 5 — Check the residuals


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
pr <- pseudoRes(m2)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
qqnorm(pr$stepRes, main = "Step pseudo-residuals", pch = 16, cex = 0.3,
       col = adjustcolor("#1f6f78", 0.4))
qqline(pr$stepRes, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
qqnorm(pr$angleRes, main = "Angle pseudo-residuals", pch = 16, cex = 0.3,
       col = adjustcolor("#1f6f78", 0.4))
qqline(pr$angleRes, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Reading a pseudo-residual plot

If the model describes the data, pseudo-residuals are standard normal and the
points lie on the line. Departures tell you *where* the model fails:

- **Heavy tails** — the step-length distribution is wrong (try log-normal or
  Weibull), or outliers remain
- **Systematic curvature** — the wrong number of states, or a state whose
  distribution family does not match
- **Structure when plotted against time** — a covariate is missing: perhaps
  behaviour depends on time of day and you have not let it

This is the HMM equivalent of plotting residuals in a regression, and it is
skipped in far too many papers.
:::

## Task 6 — A different kind of segmentation

Leo the vulture needs **change-point** thinking, not state classification. The
question is *when did migration start*, and the NSD profile from Class 4 is
enough to answer it.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
vul <- read.csv("data/vulture_leo.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(t = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
            x = location.long, y = location.lat) |>
  filter(!is.na(x)) |> distinct(t, .keep_all = TRUE) |> arrange(t)

vt <- make_track(vul, x, y, t, crs = 4326) |> transform_coords(crs_to = 6933)

daily <- vt |>
  mutate(day = as.Date(t_)) |>
  group_by(day) |>
  summarise(x = mean(x_), y = mean(y_), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(day) |>
  mutate(disp_km = c(NA, sqrt(diff(x)^2 + diff(y)^2)) / 1000)

daily <- daily |> mutate(migrating = disp_km > 50)

plot(daily$day, daily$disp_km, type = "h",
     col = ifelse(daily$migrating, "#c1440e", "grey65"),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Daily displacement (km)",
     main = "Leo: daily displacement, migration days in red")
abline(h = 50, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-align='center' width=864}
:::
:::


### Your turn

**6a.** How many migration days per year, and in which months?
**6b.** Why is a simple threshold acceptable here, when it would not be for the buffalo?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
daily |>
  filter(migrating) |>
  count(year = year(day), name = "migration_days")
#> # A tibble: 7 × 2
#>    year migration_days
#>   <dbl>          <int>
#> 1  2007             57
#> 2  2008             85
#> 3  2009             80
#> 4  2010             67
#> 5  2011             40
#> 6  2012             13
#> 7  2013              5

daily |>
  filter(migrating) |>
  count(month = month(day, label = TRUE), name = "days")
#> # A tibble: 9 × 2
#>   month  days
#>   <ord> <int>
#> 1 Jan       6
#> 2 Feb       6
#> 3 Mar      47
#> 4 Apr      84
#> 5 May       5
#> 6 Sep      12
#> 7 Oct     109
#> 8 Nov      66
#> 9 Dec      12
```
:::


Migration days cluster strongly in the **spring and autumn** months, exactly
as the NSD sawtooth in Class 4 suggested.

**Why a threshold is defensible here.** The two behaviours are separated by
roughly an order of magnitude: a resident vulture moves a few kilometres a
day, a migrating one moves hundreds. The distribution of daily displacement is
clearly bimodal with a wide, empty valley between the modes, so the exact
threshold barely matters.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
hist(log10(daily$disp_km + 1), breaks = 50, col = "#1f6f78", border = "white",
     xlab = "log10(daily displacement km + 1)", main = "Two clearly separated modes")
abline(v = log10(51), col = "firebrick", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){fig-align='center' width=624}
:::
:::


For the buffalo there is no such valley: resting, grazing and travelling
produce overlapping step-length distributions with no gap to cut at. That is
precisely when you need a model that assigns states probabilistically and uses
the time dependence to resolve the overlap — an HMM.

**The general rule:** if a histogram of your metric shows a clean gap, a
threshold is honest and transparent. If it does not, a threshold is an
arbitrary decision dressed as a result.
:::

## Self-check

::: {.quiz}
Your 2-state HMM assigns 97% of steps to state 1 and 3% to state 2, and state
2 has a mean step length of 12 km. What has probably happened?

- [ ] The animal genuinely travels 3% of the time
- [x] State 2 is absorbing location errors rather than describing a behaviour
- [ ] The model needs more states
- [ ] The sampling interval is too short

::: {.quiz-feedback}
A rare state with an extreme mean is the classic signature of a model mopping
up **outliers**. Twelve kilometres in one step is implausible for most
terrestrial mammals at an hourly interval, and the HMM has done what it was
asked to do: found the mixture that best fits the data, including the bad
points.

Clean first, then model. Find the offending steps, look at them on a map,
decide whether they are real, and remove them (or the affected bursts) before
refitting. This is why Task 1 drops the 63 km steps.

More states would not help — you would simply get more outlier-absorbing
states.
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
You want to know whether buffalo are more likely to start moving when it is
hot. What do you change in `fitHMM()`?

- [ ] Add temperature to `stepPar0`
- [x] Pass `formula = ~ temperature` so the covariate acts on the transition probabilities
- [ ] Fit separate models for hot and cold days
- [ ] Nothing — HMMs cannot include covariates

::: {.quiz-feedback}
The question is about **switching between behaviours**, and switching is
governed by the transition probability matrix. `formula = ~ temperature` makes
the transition probabilities a (multinomial-logit) function of temperature,
which is exactly the hypothesis.

Putting a covariate on the *state-dependent distributions* instead would ask a
different question — "does the animal travel faster when it is hot", given
that it is already travelling.

Fitting separate models for hot and cold days throws away the transitions
between them and gives you no test of the difference.

This is where Class 5 and Class 6 join up: annotate each fix with the
contemporaneous covariate, then let it drive the transitions.
:::
:::

## Before Class 7

- **Read Fieberg et al. (2021)**, *J Anim Ecol* 90:1027–1043. Genuinely the
  most useful paper in this course.
- Make sure `library(amt)` and `library(survival)` both load.
